name: Karl Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Karl. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes back to your company with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a team of eight claims handlers at Harbourline, a big home insurance company, in their office above the shopping centre on Station Road. I got the team-leader job eight months ago, mostly because nobody else applied, and honestly I'm still learning it. My day is the morning huddle at half eight, then signing off claims over the limit, chasing the ones that have gone past thirty days, and sitting in on difficult calls. What wears me out is the spreadsheets for head office every Friday; what I like is when Denise, who's been there twenty years, tells me I handled a call well.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you're still learning it. What's the hardest part of the job for you right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Saying no to people I used to sit next to. Six months ago I was one of them, eating lunch with them in the break room, and now I'm the one telling Marcus his call times are too long. And the systems keep changing on me; there's a new claims screen every year and I'm always the last to figure it out. I don't use any of the AI stuff, the chat assistant they put on our laptops, I just switch it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the five pictures. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so. Half of what gets sold as AI is the same old automation with a new label, and I'd say that in the pub without blinking. At work I'd keep my mouth shut, because the regional director loves all that stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I still have to get good at this job, which I'm not yet. The thing that worries me isn't robots, it's that I'm the weakest team leader on the floor and Harbourline restructures every two years anyway. Lena, my partner, and I pay 1,150 a month in rent, and I've got about three months put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and finish the team-leader course the company pays for, the one I keep putting off. I'd go back to putting 200 a month into savings, which stopped when the car needed a clutch. And I'd finally say yes when the union rep asks me to come to a branch meeting, because restructures happen with or without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with a bit of the usual Sunday-night dread. Nothing changes, but nothing changing still means I'm on probation in my own head every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned restructures every two years. What happened last time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They merged two teams on the third floor and one of the team leaders, Gary, got told on a Tuesday and was gone by the Friday. He had a mortgage and a baby on the way, and the email said 'simplifying our structure'. I helped him carry his box to the car park, and I remember thinking, that's the job I'm doing now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena about all this over dinner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're fine for now, which is what I always say. She works nights on a hospital ward, so she's heard worse, and she'd tell me to stop catastrophising. My boss can cut my team, but nobody's cutting Lena's ward.

say: AI is mostly **old automation** with a new label, and I'd say so to my friends.
At work I'd **stay quiet**, because the regional director is keen on the stuff.
think: The real threat is that I'm the **weakest team leader** on the floor.
Harbourline **restructures** every two years with or without AI, so I'm never fully safe.
With **three months saved** and 1,150 rent, one bad restructure would hurt.
do: Finish the **team-leader course** that the company pays for and that I keep putting off.
Restart saving **200 a month** now the car clutch is paid for.
Go to a **union branch meeting** when the rep next asks.
feel: Mostly **relief**, with the usual Sunday-night dread about being found out.
S0.quote: My boss can cut my team, but nobody's cutting Lena's ward.
fieldNote: Even with AI flat, his worry is **restructuring**, not technology; he watched Gary go in four days.
Leans on **Lena's nursing job** as the household's real safety net.
Admits he **switches off** the AI assistant, which matters a lot in later scenarios.

steps.text: Finish the company-paid team-leader course by spring
Put 200 a month back into the savings account
Attend the next union branch meeting at the Station Road office

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that these tools should help people do the job, not replace them, and the union needs a seat at the table. I'd probably share the union's posts about it online. I wouldn't say any of that to the regional director's face though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, claims handling is exactly the kind of work this eats: reading a form, checking it against the policy, writing a letter. If the software does that, Harbourline doesn't need eight handlers, it needs three, and it doesn't need me to manage three. I'm the one who refuses to touch the AI tools, so I'd be the obvious team leader to drop when they merge teams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the 80-a-month gym and the takeaways straight away and push the savings to five or six months. I'd get properly involved with the union, maybe even stand as a workplace rep, because reps get consulted before cuts. And I'd ask HR what happens to team leaders when teams shrink, in writing, so I've got it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, honestly. It feels like watching a queue get shorter when you're near the front of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the obvious one to drop. Would you start using the AI tools to avoid that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know I should, and I hate that I know it. I've watched Priti on the next team use it to draft settlement letters and it's quick, but half the time she's fixing its mistakes. I'd probably learn the bare minimum if my manager made it a target, but I wouldn't volunteer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Denise, without a doubt. She's fifty-two, she's brilliant on the phone, and she's never used anything newer than the old claims system. If they offered voluntary redundancy she'd take it and then struggle to get anything else, and I'd be the one handing her the letter.

say: AI should **help people**, not replace them, and the **union** needs a seat at the table.
I'd share the **union's posts** online but stay quiet in front of the director.
think: Reading forms and writing letters is **exactly the work** this software eats.
Eight handlers become three, and three don't need **a team leader** like me.
Refusing the AI tools makes me the **obvious one** to drop.
do: Cancel the **80-a-month gym** and the takeaways in the first month.
Build savings up to **five or six months** of costs within the year.
Stand as a **workplace union rep** so I'm consulted before any cuts.
feel: A **tight chest**, like being near the front of a shrinking queue.
S1.quote: If the software does that, Harbourline doesn't need eight handlers, it needs three, and it doesn't need me to manage three.
fieldNote: Sees clearly that **claims work** sits in the path of thinking AI.
Gap between **say and think**: public line is about fairness, private fear is personal.
Would learn AI **only under orders**; his resistance is part pride, part fear.
His concern for **Denise** shows a protective streak towards older staff.

steps.text: Cancel the gym membership and stop weekday takeaways
Build savings to five months of rent and bills
Stand for workplace union rep at the Harbourline office

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest grab by companies in history and governments have to step in, with things like a basic income paid for by taxing the firms using it. I'd be marching, I think, for the first time in my life. At work I'd say the union has to negotiate proper redundancy terms now, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be out of a job by 2028, maybe sooner, because there'd be nothing left for my team to do and nothing for me to manage. Two years isn't enough time to retrain into anything that isn't also about to go, and I'm not the type to land on my feet. The robots coming three years later only buys time for people who work with their hands, and I've sat at a desk my whole working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd go to the union and push for a redundancy deal, and I'd keep every penny of whatever payout came. Lena and I would look at moving somewhere cheaper, maybe back near my mum, so the rent drops. I'd look at hands-on jobs that might hold out till 2031, like the hospital porter roles Lena keeps mentioning, even though that's a pay cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like the floor's gone, and I'm the sort of person who needs a floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hands-on work buys three years. What would that mean for you, someone who's always been at a desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about it since you read it out. Lena's ward will still need people lifting and washing patients till the robots come, and porters, and cleaners. I could do that, I'm not proud. Hospital portering would be a three-year stay of execution, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if the payout ran low?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, before anything. Then we'd stop sending money to my sister for her course, which would break my heart. Rent is the one we can't cut without moving, so moving would come quickly.

say: This is the **biggest grab** by companies ever, and government must tax it into a **basic income**.
The union has to win **redundancy terms** now, before the job cuts land.
think: I'd be **out of a job** by 2028, with nothing left for my team to do.
Two years isn't enough to **retrain** into something that isn't also going.
Robots coming later only helps **hands-on workers**, and I've always been at a desk.
do: Push the union for a **redundancy deal** and save the whole payout.
Move with Lena **somewhere cheaper**, maybe near my mum, to drop the rent.
Apply for **hospital porter** jobs that might last until 2031.
feel: **Sick**, as if the floor has gone from under me.
Ashamed that I'm **not the type** to land on my feet.
S2.quote: Hospital portering would be a three-year stay of execution, not a career.
fieldNote: Expects to **lose his job** outright; mood is driven by that, not by how calm he sounds.
Sees the **three-year robot gap** only as a short refuge for hands-on work.
Would turn to **protest and politics** for the first time; his outlook turns fear outward.
Would cut **support to his sister** before rent, which clearly hurts him.

steps.text: Push the union to win a redundancy deal before cuts
Apply for hospital porter jobs at Lena's hospital
Move near his mum to halve the rent
Sell the car once the payout starts running low

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to get the rules right, so let's not waste them like we wasted the warnings on everything else. I'd be loud about it in the union and probably online. I'd want the company to commit to retraining people before it lets anyone go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd see it coming instead of getting hit, which is the only real difference for me. My job still goes, probably around 2030 as the tools get closer. But I'd be thirty-two, not twenty-nine, with time to train for something that holds out longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for a part-time course, probably something like a healthcare assistant qualification, since Lena says the wards will always be short. I'd keep pushing savings up, aiming for six months, and I'd use the union to get Harbourline to pay for retraining. I'd keep the team-leader job as long as it lasts and not jump early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still scared, but it's a slower kind of scared. I could sleep, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you're not the type to land on your feet. Does five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'm slow with new things, so five years suits me better than two, because I can learn one thing properly instead of panicking. Being slow isn't the same as being stupid, I just need longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Denise if she asked you what to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Denise to take any retraining money the moment it's offered, because she won't get a second go at fifty-seven. I'd feel a hypocrite saying it, since I'd be dragging my own feet. But I'd mean it.

say: We have **five years** to get the rules right, so let's not waste them.
Harbourline should **pay for retraining** before anyone is let go.
think: My job still goes, probably **around 2030**, but I'd see it coming.
At thirty-two I'd have time to train for work that **holds out longer**.
do: Start a **part-time healthcare assistant** course within the first year.
Push savings up to **six months** of costs.
Press the union to make Harbourline **fund retraining** for staff.
feel: Still **scared**, but slower, so I could mostly sleep.
S3.quote: Being slow isn't the same as being stupid, I just need longer.
fieldNote: Extra time matters to him because he **learns slowly**, not because the end point changes.
Still expects to **lose the desk job**, so the mood stays high despite better sleep.
Healthcare plan is shaped by **Lena's ward** and the later arrival of robots.
Notices his own **hypocrisy** in advising Denise to move first.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time healthcare assistant course this year
Raise savings to six months of rent and bills
Press the union to make Harbourline fund staff retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly if governments actually plan, with retraining money and shorter weeks shared out. I'd vote for whoever promised that, and I'd say so. At work I'd keep my head down and do the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is a career. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, and I'd probably have been pushed sideways once or twice before then anyway. I think I'd stay at Harbourline for a few years, watch what the others do, and move when it's obvious, which is how I do everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one, honestly, not much: I'd stay put, keep saving, and keep going to union meetings. Maybe year three I'd start the healthcare course. I'd vote and campaign for the party promising retraining funds and a shorter working week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but there's a guilt to it, because I know I'd waste some of the ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste some of the ten years. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's me. I left the team-leader course for eight months even though it was free and in work time. Give me ten years and I'll spend the first four telling myself there's plenty of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Lena change any plans, like buying a home or having kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about kids around thirty. With ten years I think we'd still go for it, but we'd want Lena's job to be the steady one, which it already is. We'd probably hold off buying, because I wouldn't want a mortgage on my salary.

say: Ten years is enough if government plans **retraining money** and **shorter weeks**.
I'd vote for whoever promised that, and keep my **head down** at work.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** when it lands, which is a career away.
I'd stay, **watch the others**, and move only when it's obvious.
do: Stay at Harbourline and keep **saving monthly** through the first year.
Vote and campaign for the party offering **retraining funds**.
Hold off **buying a home** while keeping plans for children around thirty.
feel: **Calmer**, with some guilt that I'd waste part of the decade.
S4.quote: Give me ten years and I'll spend the first four telling myself there's plenty of time.
fieldNote: Knows his own **procrastination** and names it frankly.
Ten years turns fear into **waiting**; he plans to move only once others have.
Family plans hinge on **Lena's job** as the steady income.
Still expects to lose the role eventually, so **anxious** rather than uneasy.

steps.text: Stay in the Harbourline team-leader job and watch for signals
Campaign for the party promising retraining funds and shorter weeks
Delay buying a home until his own income looks safer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years is no time for someone like me who needs ages to learn anything. What would help is a law that makes companies give a year's notice and pay for retraining, and a union that's strong enough to make them stick to it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd tell my team. I wouldn't, at first, and that bothers me. If I knew the cuts were coming I think I'd sit on it to keep things calm, and I'd hate myself for it.

headlineQuote: I'm slow with new things, so five years suits me better than two, because I can learn one thing properly instead of panicking.
portrait: Karl is a **twenty-seven-year-old** claims team leader at a large home insurer, eight months into the role.
He feels like the **weakest team leader** on the floor and switches off the AI assistant.
His safety net is his partner **Lena's nursing job** and about three months of savings.
He turns fear into **union and politics**, but admits he waits until others move first.
He moves from **uneasy** with no change to **alarmed** under fast AGI, easing slightly with time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short for someone who learns slowly.
whatWouldHelp: A law requiring **a year's notice** and company-paid retraining.
A **strong union** able to enforce those terms.
